column2: NIV suits a conscious COPD patient with persistent hypercapnic acidosis; confusion, profound hypoxia, undrained pneumothorax and secretions favour intubation.
LTOT ≥ 15 h/day improved survival in hypoxaemic COPD with cor pulmonale (MRC, NOTT); no survival benefit shown in CF, IPF or sarcoid.
Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.67 with low transfer factor is COPD with emphysema; asbestosis would be restrictive.
Copious purulent sputum, coarse basal crackles and clubbing after severe childhood measles is post-infective bronchiectasis; HRCT confirms.
Severe childhood measles, pertussis or TB damage bronchial walls, causing post-infectious bronchiectasis.
Cystic fibrosis (thick mucus from CFTR defect) causes bronchiectasis in the young; also consider ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, ABPA.
Haemoptysis is common in bronchiectasis (enlarged bronchial arteries); massive bleeding may need bronchial artery embolisation.
The signet-ring sign (bronchus wider than its artery) is the key HRCT sign of bronchiectasis; honeycombing means fibrotic ILD.
Chronic infection and neutrophilic inflammation of dilated bronchi cause the large daily sputum volumes; airway clearance is central.
Persistent daily sputum in bronchiectasis needs daily airway clearance (e.g. oscillating PEP flutter device) taught by a physiotherapist.
Bronchiectasis exacerbations are reduced by daily airway clearance (postural drainage); add long-term azithromycin if ≥ 3 exacerbations/year.
Chronic purulent sputum and coarse basal crackles in rheumatoid arthritis is bronchiectasis; RA-ILD gives a dry cough and fine crackles.
Months of cough, fever, sweats and weight loss with upper-zone shadowing is TB: 2–3 sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and Xpert MTB/RIF.
Jaundice weeks into RIPE therapy is drug-induced hepatitis; stop if ALT > 5× normal, then reintroduce drugs one at a time.
Diabetes is an associated disease raising TB risk (like HIV, steroids, CKD, silicosis); contact, overcrowding and smoking are patient factors.
Most pulmonary TB is treated as outpatients; admit for uncertain diagnosis, intolerance, poor adherence, severe illness or MDR-TB. Diabetes alone is not a reason.
Drug resistance comes from inadequate treatment and non-adherence (previous treatment is the strongest predictor); diabetes is not a cause.
CURB-65 = 5 with multilobar disease and high lactate is high-severity pneumonia: early ICU review, IV co-amoxiclav plus clarithromycin.
Pyrazinamide causes both hepatitis and hyperuricaemia/gout; isoniazid causes neuropathy, rifampicin cholestasis, ethambutol optic neuritis.
High-resolution CT confirms bronchiectasis (signet ring, no tapering); then test for a cause (immunoglobulins, ABPA, CF, cilia).
Rising PaCO2 in pneumonia means the patient is tiring: an indication for ICU assessment. CURB-65 of 2 is ward care.
Primary TB may cause hypersensitivity: erythema nodosum and phlyctenular conjunctivitis, with a Ghon focus and hilar nodes.
A heavy drinker with foul sputum and a right lower-lobe cavity with air–fluid level has an aspiration lung abscess; prolonged antibiotics with anaerobic cover.
Primary TB can cause erythema nodosum, phlyctenular conjunctivitis and dactylitis; erythema marginatum belongs to rheumatic fever.
S. pneumoniae is the commonest cause of lobar pneumonia; the fever often reactivates herpes labialis (cold sores).
IGRA cannot separate latent from active TB and is often positive in high-prevalence countries; sputum smear, culture and Xpert diagnose active disease.
CURB-65 = 2 with penicillin allergy: doxycycline or clarithromycin (amoxicillin otherwise).
S. aureus pneumonia is necrotising and bacteraemic, seeding metastatic abscesses including brain abscess.
TB risk is highest in young children and the elderly; age 20–25 is not a risk factor.
TB granulomas contain epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells and lymphocytes with caseation; neutrophils are not characteristic.
Fever, sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis in a young adult is pulmonary TB until proven otherwise; send sputum for AFB.
Sputum AFB smear and culture (± molecular test) is the key test for pulmonary TB; culture is the gold standard and gives sensitivities.
Dullness, bronchial breathing and reduced expansion in one zone with fever and purulent sputum are the signs of lobar consolidation.
S. pneumoniae is the commonest identified cause of community-acquired pneumonia and classic lobar consolidation.
Low-severity pneumonia (CURB-65 0–1): oral amoxicillin 500 mg tds for 5 days; doxycycline or clarithromycin if allergic.
Chronic productive cough, clubbing and male infertility suggest bronchiectasis from CF, primary ciliary dyskinesia or Young syndrome.
Overbreathing healthy alveoli removes CO2 but cannot add oxygen to saturated blood, so shunt through consolidation causes type 1 failure.
TB control: case-finding, DOT, isolation, contact tracing with preventive therapy and BCG. Pneumococcal vaccine has no effect on TB.
Mild transaminase rises are common early in TB treatment but serious hepatitis is rare; isoniazid neuropathy, ethambutol optic neuritis.
Nasal disease then haemoptysis with multiple cavitating nodules is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3).
Cavitation indicates active, usually smear-positive, post-primary TB; calcified nodes and fibrosis are old disease.
S. pneumoniae is a Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococcus; clusters mean staphylococci.
Lobar pneumonia gives homogeneous consolidation bounded by fissures, with air bronchograms and a silhouette sign.
Extensive left airspace opacity with air bronchograms and preserved volume is consolidation; hotel travel and confusion suggest Legionella.
Confusion (1) + urea > 7 (1) = CURB-65 2: moderate severity, hospital treatment with amoxicillin plus clarithromycin; send Legionella antigen.
Hotel water systems, confusion, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and deranged LFTs suggest Legionella; urinary antigen, treat with a macrolide or quinolone.
Patchy left basal opacity obscuring the hemidiaphragm is left lower-lobe consolidation; with cold sores, typical pneumococcal pneumonia.
Hotel stay plus a sick contact: multiplex PCR on sputum/swab rapidly detects Legionella, influenza and other pathogens.
